passage:
Monday. Before I even tried, I typed the whole assignment question into the AI. Even the email to the hostel warden. Dhruv, that's me, apparently. It felt faster, though it took me twenty minutes to figure out what I'd actually been asked to do.

Thursday. Manoj asked in class how our project's sorting step worked. I opened my mouth and there was nothing. My own thinking felt slow and rusty, like a bicycle left out in the rain. I said "I'll get back to you," which was true and embarrassing.

Next Tuesday. I set a timer for fifteen minutes and tried the problem on paper first. It was messy but mine. Then I asked the AI to check my steps and explain one I'd missed. This time I could explain it to Manoj at lunch.

qa.q: What did Manoj ask about in class on Thursday?
qa.a: Manoj asked how the project's sorting step worked.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when the answer would not come on Thursday?
qa.a: Dhruv felt slow and rusty, like a bicycle left out in the rain, and embarrassed to say "I'll get back to you".

qa.q: What changed on Tuesday, and why is it a wiser way to use AI?
qa.a: Dhruv tried the problem on paper for fifteen minutes first, then asked the AI to check and explain a missed step, so the skill stayed Dhruv's own.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Dhruv's silence on Thursday and the explanation later?
qa.a: Manoj may have been surprised by the silence, but the clear explanation at lunch showed Dhruv now understood the step, not just the answer.

grounding: Dhruv asks the AI before trying and feels slower, then over days tries first, uses AI to check and can explain the work.
